title: Pronoun-antecedent agreement
blurb: Make every pronoun match its antecedent in number and person, including compound antecedents, things and organizations.
question: A clinic newsletter says, “The lab and the pharmacy will extend it's hours, so if a patient needs a refill, you can come after work.” How many pronoun agreement errors are there, and how would you fix each one?

teach.h: A pronoun must match the word it replaces
teach.body: Formally, a pronoun agrees with its antecedent (the noun it replaces) in number (singular or plural), person (first, second or third) and, where it is stated, gender. Plain English: find the word the pronoun points back to, then check that the pronoun is the same size (one or many) and speaks from the same point of view. “The nurses finished their charts” agrees; “The nurses finished her charts” does not.

head: Match
Antecedent
Pronoun
teach.caption: Find the antecedent first. The pronoun copies its number and person, not the number of a nearby noun.

children.label: Plural pronoun
children.sub: The cuff and the scale need their batteries.

children.label: Match the nearer one
children.sub: Neither the nurse nor the aides lost their badges.

teach.caption: “And” adds the antecedents together. “Or” and “nor” offer a choice, so the antecedent closer to the pronoun decides.

teach.body: Each, every, either, neither and one are singular. When they refer to things, the pronoun is it or its: “Each of the vials must be checked before it is used.” Both, few, many and several are plural: “Several of the monitors lost their signal.” For people, current US usage accepts “Everyone brought their badge,” so it is never the error the HESI A2 is looking for. Look for clear number clashes with plural nouns and things instead.

teach.h: Things and organizations take it and its
teach.caption: Its is the possessive and never takes an apostrophe. It's always means “it is” or “it has.”

Pronouns

rows: I, me, my, we, us, our
teach.caption: A person shift moves from one row to another for the same people: “When one studies, you remember more.”

rows.label: The lab and the pharmacy changed its hours.
Neither Mr. Ruiz nor the aides brought their badges.
If a patient feels dizzy, you should sit down.
Each of the rooms has its own sink.

teach.h: Scenario: Priya edits the clinic newsletter
teach.body: Nursing applicant Priya Shah volunteers on a clinic newsletter. The draft says: “The lab and the pharmacy will extend it's hours, so if a patient needs a refill, you can come after work.” Two antecedents joined by and are plural, so it's becomes their. The second clause shifts from a patient (third person) to you (second person), so she writes patients ... they. Final: “The lab and the pharmacy will extend their hours, so patients who need a refill can come after work.”

teach.text: The pronoun agrees with its antecedent, not with the nearest noun. In “Each of the monitors needs ___ screen cleaned,” the plural monitors sits right next to the blank, but the antecedent is each, so the answer is its. The other classic HESI A2 traps are it's written for its and a sentence that slides from a patient or one into you.

items: Find the antecedent, then match it in number (one or many) and person (first, second, third).
Antecedents joined by and take a plural pronoun; with or or nor, the nearer antecedent decides.
Each, every, either, neither and one are singular: with things they take it or its.
Both, few, many and several are plural: they take they, them and their.
An organization or committee acting as one unit takes its, never it's.
Do not shift from a patient, one or students to you or we.

summary: You can now make a pronoun match its antecedent in number and person, including antecedents joined by and, or and nor. You can also give things and organizations its, spot it's used as a possessive, and fix sentences that shift from third person to you.

A.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The two surgeons reviewed ___ notes before the first case.”
A.why: The antecedent “surgeons” is plural, so the plural possessive “their” agrees.

whyNot.0: “His” is singular, but the antecedent “surgeons” is plural.
whyNot.2: “They're” means “they are”; the sentence needs a possessive before “notes.”
whyNot.3: “Her” is singular, but the antecedent “surgeons” is plural.

A.q: Which sentence about checking in keeps the same person throughout?
options: When you arrive at the clinic, you should check in at the desk.
When a patient arrives at the clinic, you should check in at the desk.
When one arrives at the clinic, you should check in at the desk.
When we arrive at the clinic, you should check in at the desk.
A.why: Both pronouns are second person (you ... you), so the point of view stays the same.

whyNot.1: It shifts from third person (“a patient”) to second person (“you”).
whyNot.2: It shifts from third person (“one”) to second person (“you”).
whyNot.3: It shifts from first person (“we”) to second person (“you”).

A.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The laboratory upgraded ___ testing equipment last year.”
A.why: A laboratory is one thing, so it takes the singular possessive “its,” with no apostrophe.

whyNot.0: “It's” means “it is” or “it has,” not a possessive.
whyNot.1: “They're” means “they are” and is plural; the laboratory needs “its.”
whyNot.3: “Its'” is not a word: possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe.

B.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “Neither the charge nurse nor the aides had finished ___ charting by noon.”
B.why: With “neither...nor,” the pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent. “Aides” is nearer and plural, so “their” is correct.

whyNot.0: “Her” would match the farther antecedent, “charge nurse”; the nearer antecedent, “aides,” is plural.
whyNot.1: “His” is singular and matches neither the nearer antecedent nor the plural “aides.”
whyNot.2: “Its” is for things, and the nearer antecedent, “aides,” is plural people.

B.q: Which sentence about cleaning equipment shows correct agreement with a compound antecedent?
options: The gloves and the gown go in the bin after you remove it.
The gauze and the tape are low, so please reorder it.
The scale and the cuff were cleaned, and they are ready.
The cart and the pump need cleaning before it is used.
B.why: “The scale and the cuff” is joined by “and,” so the plural “they” agrees.

whyNot.0: “The gloves and the gown” is plural, so the pronoun must be “them.”
whyNot.1: “The gauze and the tape” is plural, so the pronoun must be “them.”
whyNot.3: “The cart and the pump” is plural, so the clause must read “before they are used.”

B.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “Each of the exam rooms has ___ own sink and supply cabinet.”
B.why: “Each” is singular and the rooms are things, so the singular possessive “its” agrees.

whyNot.0: “Their” is plural; it matches “rooms,” but the antecedent is the singular “each.”
whyNot.1: “It's” means “it is”; the sentence needs the possessive “its.”
whyNot.2: “There” names a place; the sentence needs a possessive pronoun.

C.q: Which revision corrects every error in “Every one of the IV pumps need their battery checked”?
options: Every one of the IV pumps needs its battery checked.
Every one of the IV pumps need its battery checked.
Every one of the IV pumps needs it's battery checked.
Every one of the IV pumps needs their battery checked.
C.why: Two fixes: “Every one” is singular, so the verb is “needs,” and a single pump (a thing) takes “its.”

whyNot.1: “Its” is fixed, but the verb “need” still disagrees with the singular “every one.”
whyNot.2: The verb is fixed, but “it's” means “it is,” not the possessive “its.”
whyNot.3: The verb is fixed, but “their” is plural and refers to a single pump.

C.q: Which sentence from a visitor guide contains a pronoun agreement error?
options: The interns and the residents posted their schedules.
The pharmacy updated its hours for the holiday weekend.
If students arrive late, they must sign in at the desk.
If a visitor feels unwell, you should tell a nurse.
C.why: The sentence shifts from third person (“a visitor”) to second person (“you”).

whyNot.0: Correct: “interns and residents” is plural and “their” is plural.
whyNot.1: Correct: the pharmacy is one organization, so “its” agrees.
whyNot.2: Correct: “students” and “they” are both third person plural.

C.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “Either the old monitors or the new pump will lose ___ charge first.”
C.why: With “either...or,” the pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent. “Pump” is nearer and singular, so “its” is correct.

whyNot.0: “Their” matches the farther antecedent, “monitors”; the nearer one, “pump,” is singular.
whyNot.2: “It's” means “it is” and cannot show possession.

reteach.title: A pronoun is a stand-in actor
reteach.question: In a play, a stand-in takes over when the lead actor steps out. What must be true about the stand-in so the audience is not confused?

blocks.h: The stand-in must match the lead
blocks.body: If the lead role is a group of five nurses, one stand-in cannot play all five: the pronoun must be plural (they, their). If the lead is a single thing, such as a clinic or a pump, the stand-in is it or its. And the stand-in must speak from the same seat in the theater: if the play is told about a patient (third person), the stand-in cannot suddenly talk to the audience as you.

blocks.text: The audience follows the lead, not the actor standing nearest the stage. A plural noun in an “of” phrase (each of the rooms) does not change who the lead is.

explain.body: A singular antecedent takes a singular pronoun; a plural antecedent takes a plural pronoun. Things take it and its; groups of things take they and their.

test.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The infusion pumps must have ___ settings checked every morning.”
test.why: The antecedent “pumps” is plural, so the plural possessive “their” agrees.

explain.body: Two antecedents joined by and are plural. With or, nor, either...or and neither...nor, the pronoun matches the nearer antecedent.

test.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The blood pressure cuff and the thermometer were cleaned, and ___ are back on the cart.”
test.why: “The cuff and the thermometer” is joined by “and,” so the antecedent is plural, and the subject form “they” is needed.

whyNot.0: “It” is singular, but two items joined by “and” are plural.
whyNot.1: “Them” is plural but is an object form; the blank is the subject of “are.”
whyNot.3: “Its” is a singular possessive, not a subject.

explain.body: Keep the same point of view for the same people. If a sentence begins with a patient, students or one (third person), it cannot switch to you (second person) or we (first person).

test.q: Which revision fixes the shift in “A new graduate should ask questions, because you learn faster that way”?
options: New graduates should ask questions, because they learn faster that way.
New graduates should ask questions, because you learn faster that way.
A new graduate should ask questions, because we learn faster that way.
New graduates should ask questions, because one learns faster that way.
test.why: “New graduates” and “they” are both third person plural.

whyNot.1: It still shifts from third person (“graduates”) to second person (“you”).
whyNot.2: It shifts from third person (“a new graduate”) to first person (“we”).
whyNot.3: “One” is singular and generic, so it no longer refers to the plural “graduates.”

explain.body: A clinic, hospital or committee acting as one unit takes the singular possessive its. Its never has an apostrophe; it's always means it is or it has.

test.q: Which sentence about the clinic's new hours is correct?
options: The clinic posted it's new hours on the door.
The clinic posted its' new hours on the door.
The clinic posted its new hours on the door.
The clinics posted its new hours on the door.
test.why: One clinic takes the singular possessive “its,” written with no apostrophe.

whyNot.0: “It's” means “it is”; the sentence needs the possessive “its.”
whyNot.3: “Clinics” is plural, so the pronoun must be “their.”
